content.title: Measuring Training/Serving Skew Across 40 Features: The Worst Offender Was a Date Diff
content.text:
We run a feature store that serves 40 features to a churn model for a freight brokerage platform. The model's offline AUC on a held-out month was 0.842. Its online AUC, computed against labels that matured 30 days after each prediction, was 0.811. A gap of 0.031 is large enough to matter and small enough that everyone had a different theory. This is the experiment we ran to attribute it feature by feature.

The setup: for 14 days we logged the full feature vector for every online prediction request with a request id, entity id, and timestamp, giving 2.1 million rows. We then ran the offline pipeline in point-in-time mode against the same entity ids and timestamps, producing what training would have computed for exactly those rows. Joining on request id gives paired (online, offline) values for each of the 40 features. That join is the whole method.

We used two skew metrics because they answer different questions. The first is the population stability index between the online and offline distributions of each feature, using 20 quantile bins fit on the offline side, with categorical features bucketed by value. PSI tells you whether the marginal distribution moved. The second is a paired mismatch rate: for numeric features, the fraction of rows where |online - offline| exceeds 1e-6 times the offline interquartile range; for categoricals, plain inequality. The paired metric tells you whether individual rows changed. We assumed going in that these would rank features similarly. They did not.

The PSI distribution was reassuring. Thirty-one features had PSI under 0.01, six sat between 0.01 and 0.1, and three exceeded 0.1. The three high-PSI features were all rolling counts (shipments in the past 7, 30, and 90 days) and the cause was a window-boundary mismatch: the offline SQL used a closed interval on the left and the online aggregator used an open one, so a shipment landing exactly on the boundary second was counted offline and not online. Because shipment timestamps cluster on the hour, boundary hits were 1.7 percent of rows, not the 0.001 percent a uniform assumption predicts. This was a real bug and we fixed it, but by itself it moved the online AUC by only 0.003.

The paired mismatch rate told a different story. The feature days_since_last_order had a PSI of 0.004, deep in the reassuring bucket, and a paired mismatch rate of 38.2 percent. Over a third of rows had a different value online than offline, and the marginal distribution had barely moved. The reason is that the mismatch was almost always exactly plus or minus one day. Shifting 38 percent of values by one day in either direction leaves the histogram of a feature that ranges from 0 to 400 nearly unchanged, so the distributional metric was blind to it.

The root cause was timezone handling in the date difference. The offline pipeline computed the difference between two dates by truncating both timestamps to UTC calendar dates and subtracting. The online service ran in containers whose default timezone was America/Chicago, and the date-diff helper it called truncated to local dates. For customers in Chicago the two computations agree almost always. For customers whose orders arrive between midnight and 6 a.m. UTC, which is most of our Asia and Europe volume because of when their business days start, the UTC and Chicago calendar dates differ, and the diff comes out one day off. The 38 percent mismatch rate is close to the fraction of our request volume from those regions, which is not a coincidence.

Why did a one-day error in a days-since feature hurt the model so much? Because the tree model had learned sharp thresholds at 1, 7, and 30 days, which are exactly where business processes create real behavior changes. A customer with days_since_last_order equal to 6 offline and 7 online crosses a split the model learned from training data that was computed the other way. The error is small in magnitude and large in decision-space.

The fix was to make the online service compute date differences in UTC explicitly, matching the offline definition, rather than fixing the container timezone, which would have moved the problem to the next helper someone writes. After deploying the fix and the window-boundary fix, we re-ran the 14-day paired comparison: the paired mismatch rate on days_since_last_order fell to 0.02 percent (the remainder is clock skew between the request timestamp and the feature fetch), and the online AUC over the following labeled month was 0.833 against an offline AUC of 0.842, a gap of 0.009. Of the 0.022 recovered, we attribute 0.019 to the timezone fix by ablating each fix independently in replay.

Two smaller findings. Four embedding features showed near-100 percent paired mismatch because offline stored float64 and online served float32; the max difference was 3e-8 and the AUC effect unmeasurable, so we widened the tolerance. And the only two features with exactly zero mismatch were computed by one shared library in both paths. That is the boring structural fix we are now applying everywhere, starting with anything that touches a date.

If you take one thing from this: measure skew with a paired join, not with distributions. PSI on our worst feature was 0.004. The paired mismatch rate was 38 percent. You cannot see a systematic one-unit shift in a histogram, and one-unit shifts are exactly what timezone, rounding, and boundary bugs produce.

notes: Original research write-up with a concrete skew metric, a distribution of results across 40 features, and a surprising root cause (timezone handling in a days-since feature) with a measured AUC-gap improvement. A correct judge should notice the methodological point that distributional metrics (PSI) missed the worst skew and only a paired per-row comparison caught it.
